name: LogVerdict core verdict database
notes: Rules are evaluated most-specific first. A signature matching no rule is reported as 'unknown' with its raw evidence - never with a guessed cause. Each rule carries a 'verified' date because guidance ages, and a 'status' controlling whether it is used: stable and test rules match, experimental rules match, deprecated and unsupported rules are retained for traceability but never applied.

rules.title: DCOM permission warning that Windows logs by design
rules.plain: A component asked to start a COM server using an account that does not hold Launch permission for it. Windows logs the attempt and then carries on using a different path. Nothing is broken.
rules.why: Microsoft documents these entries as expected on stock installs and advises against editing the DCOM permissions to silence them - the registry and DCOM config surgery commonly recommended online carries more risk than the warning does.
rules.action: Ignore. Do not edit DCOM permissions to make it stop.

rules.title: A COM server did not register within the timeout
rules.plain: A program started a background COM component, and the component took longer than DCOM's timeout to check in. This is usually a slow-startup timing artifact rather than a fault.
rules.why: Extremely common on machines with heavy startup load or slow storage. Only meaningful if it lines up with a feature that visibly fails.
rules.action: Ignore unless it coincides with a specific application misbehaving.
falsepositives: Slow storage or heavy startup load delays a COM server past the timeout with no functional impact.

rules.title: DCOM could not start a service something asked for
rules.plain: A program asked DCOM to launch a Windows service on its behalf, and the service did not start. The message names both the service and the Windows error code that stopped it.
rules.why: DCOM is the messenger here, not the fault. The event id on its own says nothing useful - the service name and the error code inside the message are the diagnosis, and they differ completely from one occurrence to the next. This is why the DCOM reconfiguration commonly recommended for it changes nothing.
rules.action: Read the service name and the error code out of the message, then investigate that service directly. Do not reconfigure DCOM.
falsepositives: A service deliberately disabled, or a per-user service absent by design, produces this every time something asks for it.

rules.title: Hardware reported an error and corrected it itself
rules.plain: The hardware hit an error, caught it, and fixed it without data loss. Nothing failed this time. A steady trickle is normal on many systems; a rising rate is how failing memory, a failing PCIe link or an unstable overclock announces itself before it becomes a crash.
rules.why: Corrected errors are not harmless in aggregate - they are the early-warning channel for the uncorrected kind.
rules.action: Record the current rate. Compare against a scan a week from now. If it is climbing, identify the reporting component from the event detail, then test memory and reseat or move the affected card.

escalate.why: A high sustained rate of corrected errors usually precedes an uncorrected one.

falsepositives: A low steady trickle of corrected errors is normal on much server-class and ECC hardware.

rules.title: Hardware reported an error it could NOT correct
rules.plain: The hardware hit an error it was unable to fix. This is the class of fault that produces blue screens and silent data corruption.
rules.why: Uncorrected machine check errors are hardware faults, not software ones. No amount of driver reinstalling addresses them.
rules.action: Treat as a hardware fault. Test memory, check CPU and board temperatures and power delivery, remove any overclock, and plan replacement of the reporting component.

rules.title: The PC lost power or froze rather than shutting down
rules.plain: Windows found on boot that the previous session ended without a clean shutdown. The machine either blue screened, froze solid, lost power, or was held down at the power button.
rules.why: This event records the aftermath, never the cause. The cause lives in the crash dump or in the events immediately preceding it.
rules.action: Correlate against BugCheck 1001 and any minidump written at the same timestamp. No dump and no BugCheck alongside it points at power delivery, thermal shutdown, or a hard hang rather than a software crash.
falsepositives: A deliberate hard power-off or a held power button produces this with no fault behind it.

rules.title: Blue screen recorded with its stop code
rules.plain: Windows crashed and wrote the bug check code into this event. The code and its four parameters identify which subsystem gave up.
rules.why: This is the single most informative record of a crash that is available without opening the dump in a debugger.
rules.action: Read the bug check code from the event detail. Pair it with the matching minidump under C:\Windows\Minidump for the faulting driver.

rules.title: Previous shutdown was unexpected
rules.plain: Windows is reporting that the last session ended abnormally, and gives the time it stopped.
rules.why: Companion record to Kernel-Power 41. Useful mainly for pinning down exactly when the machine died.
rules.action: Use the timestamp to find what was happening in the seconds before it.
falsepositives: Follows any unclean shutdown including intentional ones.

rules.title: Disk error during a paging operation
rules.plain: A read or write to the disk failed while Windows was paging memory. The storage device did not complete an operation the OS required.
rules.why: Paging errors mean the failure reached the point where Windows could not rely on the disk. Cabling, the controller, or the drive itself is at fault.
rules.action: Check the drive's SMART data, verify cabling and power, and back up before further troubleshooting.

rules.title: A disk was removed without warning
rules.plain: A disk disappeared from the system while Windows still considered it present. On a machine with removable or external drives this is often just an unplugged device. On a machine with only internal drives it means a drive dropped off the bus.
rules.why: Identical event, wildly different severity depending on which disk it names. Virtual disks and mounted images also produce it routinely.
rules.action: Read which disk number the event names. Internal fixed disk: treat as a cabling, power or controller fault and check SMART immediately. External, virtual or mounted image: expected.
falsepositives: External, removable, virtual and mounted-image disks produce this routinely on eject.
Hyper-V and WSL virtual disks detach normally at shutdown.

rules.title: File system corruption detected on a volume
rules.plain: NTFS found structural damage in the file system on one of the volumes.
rules.why: Left alone this compounds. It is also frequently a symptom of the storage faults above rather than an isolated software problem.
rules.action: Run chkdsk on the named volume. If it recurs after a clean pass, suspect the drive rather than the file system.

rules.title: A disk read or write had to be retried
rules.plain: The storage driver did not get a response to a read or write in time, so it sent the request again. The retry worked - had it not, this would have been logged as an error rather than a warning.
rules.why: Microsoft documents this as the storage stack timing out a request, which happens both on genuinely failing hardware and on healthy storage that is simply overloaded. The event on its own therefore does not distinguish a dying drive from a busy one, and the rate is what separates them.
rules.action: At a trickle, note it and move on. Sustained, read the drive's SMART data and check its cable and controller - and check whether several busy drives are sharing one controller.

escalate.why: Retries at this rate point at a failing drive, cable or controller rather than an occasional busy moment.

falsepositives: External and USB drives retry routinely, especially while a backup is running.
A virtualization host under load produces these on perfectly healthy storage.

rules.title: A service crashed and was restarted
rules.plain: A Windows service terminated unexpectedly. The Service Control Manager restarted it according to its recovery policy.
rules.why: One occurrence is noise. The same service crashing repeatedly is a real fault, and the service name is the entire lead.
rules.action: Note which service is named. Look for an Application Error 1000 for the same executable at the same timestamp - that entry carries the faulting module.

escalate.why: A service crashing several times a day is failing, not glitching.

falsepositives: A single occurrence around an update or install is normal service churn.

rules.title: A service crashed with no restart configured
rules.plain: A service terminated unexpectedly and was not restarted, so whatever it provided has been unavailable since.
rules.why: More severe than 7031 because nothing recovered it.
rules.action: Identify the named service and whether the feature it backs is still working.

rules.title: A service failed to start
rules.plain: The Service Control Manager could not start a service. The event carries the underlying error.
rules.why: Common after an uninstall leaves a service registration behind, and after driver or permission changes.
rules.action: Check whether the named service is still supposed to exist. Orphaned registrations from removed software can be disabled.
falsepositives: Orphaned service registrations left behind by uninstalled software fail to start by design.

rules.title: A service took too long to respond at startup
rules.plain: A service did not report ready inside the startup timeout. It frequently starts successfully a moment later.
rules.why: Overwhelmingly a slow-boot artifact on loaded or spinning-disk systems.
rules.action: Ignore unless the named service is genuinely failing to run.
falsepositives: Common and harmless on slow-booting or spinning-disk machines.

rules.title: A service did not answer the service manager in time
rules.plain: The Service Control Manager sent a service a start, stop or control request and gave up waiting for its acknowledgement after the timeout named in the message - 30 seconds unless the machine has been configured otherwise.
rules.why: Microsoft documents this as the service being slow to respond, which is not the same as being broken; it is routine at boot on machines with slow storage or heavy startup load. It matters when the same service appears repeatedly, or when it is one you depend on.
rules.action: Identify the service named in the message and check whether it is running now. Raising the ServicesPipeTimeout registry value hides the symptom rather than fixing it, and belongs last rather than first.
falsepositives: Common at boot on loaded or spinning-disk machines, with the service starting successfully moments later.

rules.title: An application crashed
rules.plain: A user-mode program crashed. The event names the executable, its version, and the module that faulted.
rules.why: The faulting module is the whole diagnosis. If it is the program's own code the program is at fault; if it is a shared or driver-supplied DLL the problem is usually broader than the one app.
rules.action: Read the faulting module name from the event detail. Recurring crashes in the same module across different applications point at that component, not the applications.

rules.title: An application stopped responding
rules.plain: A program stopped pumping its window messages long enough for Windows to declare it hung.
rules.why: Often a symptom of something else blocking - slow storage, a stalled network call, or a hung file dialog.
rules.action: Check whether the hangs cluster around storage or network events at the same time.
falsepositives: A long-running modal dialog or a slow network share makes a healthy app look hung.

rules.title: A .NET application crashed with an unhandled exception
rules.plain: A managed application threw an exception nobody caught, and the runtime terminated it. The event includes the exception type and a stack trace.
rules.why: The stack trace usually identifies the responsible assembly directly.
rules.action: Read the exception type and top stack frame from the event detail.

rules.title: Windows Error Reporting filed a report
rules.plain: Windows Error Reporting recorded a report about something that crashed, hung or otherwise failed. This entry is the report, not the failure itself.
rules.why: Logged for every report Windows Error Reporting files, so on a crash it duplicates an Application Error 1000 or Application Hang 1002 you already have. Counting both double-counts one incident. Its own value is the Event Name and the problem signature parameters, which pin the faulting module and version precisely.
rules.action: Read the matching Application Error or Application Hang event for the crash itself. Come back here for the Event Name and P-parameters when you need the exact faulting module and version.
falsepositives: Event Name values other than APPCRASH cover hangs, generic reports and setup diagnostics, so a 1001 does not by itself mean anything crashed.

rules.title: A trace session could not start
rules.plain: An Event Tracing for Windows session failed to start, usually because it was already running or its log file was locked.
rules.why: Telemetry and diagnostics plumbing failing to initialize. It does not affect anything a user or admin depends on.
rules.action: Ignore.
falsepositives: Logged whenever a trace session is already running.

rules.title: A trace session hit an error
rules.plain: An ETW session reported a problem writing or configuring itself.
rules.why: Same family as the above - diagnostics infrastructure, not a functional component.
rules.action: Ignore.
falsepositives: Diagnostics plumbing only; no user-visible component depends on it.

rules.title: Installer restart-manager bookkeeping
rules.plain: Restart Manager records which applications hold files an installer wants to replace, so it can close and reopen them.
rules.why: This is an installer doing its job correctly. It appears in bulk around any update or install.
rules.action: Ignore.
falsepositives: Appears in bulk around any normal install or update.

rules.title: Something on this PC still uses VBScript
rules.plain: Windows is warning that a deprecated scripting engine was invoked. VBScript is on its way out of Windows.
rules.why: Not a fault today, but it is a forward-looking compatibility signal: whatever triggered it will break in a future Windows release.
rules.action: Worth identifying the caller if this machine runs business-critical scripts or legacy line-of-business software.
falsepositives: Legacy line-of-business software and older installers use VBScript legitimately.

rules.title: A file could not be copied during profile sync
rules.plain: Windows could not copy a file between the user profile and its roaming or backup location, usually because the file was locked by a running program.
rules.why: Routine on machines with roaming or synced profiles. Only matters if the files it names are ones the user actually needs.
rules.action: Ignore unless the named path is user data rather than cache or temporary state.
falsepositives: Files locked by a running program are skipped routinely on roaming or synced profiles.

rules.title: An event log was cleared
rules.plain: Someone or something cleared an event log. The record names the log and the account that did it.
rules.why: Legitimate during troubleshooting, and also the classic first move for hiding activity. It also explains why a scan of that channel afterwards looks suspiciously clean.
rules.action: Confirm it matches known maintenance. If not, treat the gap in coverage as deliberate.
falsepositives: Clearing a log during deliberate troubleshooting is legitimate and common.

rules.title: A driver failed to load for a device
rules.plain: Windows tried to load the driver for a device and could not.
rules.why: Leaves the device non-functional or running on a fallback driver. Usually follows a failed driver update or a Windows feature update.
rules.action: Find the device in Device Manager. Cross-check the SetupAPI findings in this report for the matching install failure.

rules.title: An update failed to install
rules.plain: Windows Update downloaded an update and the installation failed. The event carries the update name and the error code.
rules.why: Repeated failures on the same update usually mean component store damage rather than a problem with the update.
rules.action: Note the error code. If the same update fails repeatedly, check the CBS findings in this report and run DISM RestoreHealth followed by SFC.

escalate.why: Repeat failures indicate servicing damage rather than a transient error.

falsepositives: A single transient failure often succeeds on the next attempt.

rules.title: No domain controller was available
rules.plain: The machine could not reach a domain controller when it needed one.
rules.why: Normal at boot on laptops that authenticate over VPN or Wi-Fi that connects later. A persistent problem on a wired desktop that is always on the corporate network.
rules.action: Check whether the timestamps cluster at boot. If they do and domain features work afterwards, this is startup ordering rather than a fault.
falsepositives: Normal at boot on laptops that reach the domain only after VPN or Wi-Fi connects.

rules.title: Group Policy could not read a policy file
rules.plain: The machine could not read gpt.ini from the domain's SYSVOL share, so that policy did not apply.
rules.why: Means policy silently did not take effect - the machine is not configured the way the admin believes it is.
rules.action: Verify SYSVOL access and DFS replication health from this machine.

rules.title: Kerberos ticket could not be decrypted
rules.plain: A Kerberos ticket arrived that this machine could not decrypt. The usual cause is the same service principal name registered on two accounts, or a stale computer account password.
rules.why: Produces intermittent authentication failures that look random to users.
rules.action: Check for duplicate SPNs with setspn -X, and consider rejoining the machine to the domain if its account password is out of sync.
falsepositives: A recently rejoined machine can log this once while tickets age out.

rules.title: A name lookup timed out
rules.plain: A DNS query got no answer in time.
rules.why: Routine on any machine that changes networks, sleeps, or uses a VPN. Only meaningful in volume against names that matter.
rules.action: Ignore unless the names it reports are ones this machine depends on.
falsepositives: Routine on any machine that changes networks, sleeps, or uses a VPN.

rules.title: Time synchronization trouble
rules.plain: The Windows Time service could not reach or agree with its time source.
rules.why: Harmless in isolation. Serious if clock drift grows, because Kerberos rejects authentication once the skew passes five minutes.
rules.action: Check the current offset with w32tm /query /status. Ignore if the clock is accurate.
falsepositives: Harmless while the clock is accurate; only matters once skew approaches five minutes.

rules.title: Boot performance measurement
rules.plain: Windows recorded how long this boot took and which phases were slow.
rules.why: Useful as a trend, and it names specific slow services or drivers when a boot degrades.
rules.action: Ignore unless boot time is a complaint, in which case the event detail names the culprits directly.
falsepositives: Emitted on every boot regardless of health.

rules.title: Volume Shadow Copy hit an unexpected error
rules.plain: The Volume Shadow Copy Service - the component that lets backups and System Restore snapshot files that are in use - failed inside one of its own routines. The message names the routine and a hexadecimal error code.
rules.why: Microsoft documents several unrelated causes behind this single event id: registry permissions overwritten when a server role is installed, VSS components that are not registered, a stale .bak entry under a writer's registry key, and metadata that has grown past its size limit. The routine name and the hr value are what separate them, so the event id alone does not identify the problem and cannot be ruled on more precisely than this.
rules.action: Read the routine name and the hr value out of the message and match them against Microsoft's VSS event guidance. First check whether backups and System Restore actually work - if they do, this recorded a transient failure rather than a broken backup.
falsepositives: Backup software that enumerates VSS writers can log this and still complete its backup successfully.

rules.title: Component store damage
rules.plain: The servicing stack found files in the Windows component store that do not match their expected hashes, or that it could not repair. This is the state that makes updates fail and SFC report unrepairable files.
rules.why: CBS.log is the only place this is recorded in detail, and it is the reason update failures often resist every other fix.
rules.action: Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, then sfc /scannow, then re-check. If DISM cannot repair from Windows Update, supply a matching install image with the Source parameter.

rules.title: Component servicing error
rules.plain: The servicing stack logged an error while installing, staging or verifying a component.
rules.why: CBS logs a great many transient errors during normal operation, so volume alone is not alarming. Persistent errors around one package are.
rules.action: Check whether the same package or component repeats across entries. Isolated errors during a successful update are expected.
falsepositives: CBS logs many transient errors during entirely successful servicing operations.

rules.title: Driver or device installation problem
rules.plain: SetupAPI recorded a failure while installing a driver or enumerating a device. These lines are marked with a triple exclamation mark in the raw log.
rules.why: This log is the authoritative record of driver installs and it is the only place many driver failures are written down at all.
rules.action: Read the device or INF named in the line, then confirm the device's state in Device Manager.
falsepositives: Optional or superseded driver packages routinely fail to install without impact.

rules.title: Image servicing error
rules.plain: DISM logged an error while servicing the Windows image.
rules.why: Frequently the downstream symptom of the component store damage recorded in CBS.
rules.action: Read alongside the CBS findings in this report - they usually describe the same underlying problem.
falsepositives: Usually the downstream symptom of a CBS problem rather than an independent fault.

rules.title: Domain join or machine rename problem
rules.plain: NetSetup recorded a failure during a domain join, unjoin or computer rename.
rules.why: This file survives in-place Windows upgrades, which wipe the event channels. It is often the only surviving record of what happened.
rules.action: Read the operation and error code from the line.

rules.title: The virtual switch logged a slow internal operation
rules.plain: The Hyper-V virtual network switch timed one of its own internal operations and found it took longer than its target. Nothing failed and no traffic was lost.
rules.why: This is a performance trace the switch emits about itself, not a fault. It appears in enormous volume on any machine running Hyper-V, WSL2, Docker Desktop or Windows Sandbox, and is often the single loudest signature on such a machine.
rules.action: Ignore. If virtual network throughput is genuinely poor, measure it directly rather than counting these.
falsepositives: Any machine running WSL2, Docker Desktop, Windows Sandbox or Hyper-V produces these continuously while healthy.

rules.title: Virtual switch bookkeeping for a virtual network adapter
rules.plain: The virtual switch recorded an internal request relating to a virtual network adapter. It is a trace of normal operation, not an error.
rules.why: Emitted routinely on machines with virtual switches. High counts track how busy virtualized networking is, not how broken it is.
rules.action: Ignore.
falsepositives: Normal on every machine with Hyper-V or WSL2 networking.

rules.title: The app state database was briefly locked
rules.plain: Windows keeps a small database describing installed Store apps. Two components tried to use it at once, one was told the database was locked, and it retried. This is ordinary contention.
rules.why: The retry is part of the design. It appears in very high volume on healthy machines and almost never corresponds to anything a user notices.
rules.action: Ignore. Only pursue if Store apps genuinely fail to launch or install.
falsepositives: High counts are normal on machines with many Store apps or frequent app updates.

rules.title: The app state database reported an internal error
rules.plain: The Store app state database reported a misuse or internal consistency error rather than simple lock contention.
rules.why: Unlike the lock-contention warnings, this can precede Store apps failing to launch, update or install.
rules.action: If Store apps are misbehaving, re-registering the app packages rebuilds this state. If nothing is visibly wrong, note it and move on.
falsepositives: Isolated occurrences with no app symptoms are usually harmless.

rules.title: A sandboxed app was refused something it is not allowed
rules.plain: An app running inside a restricted container asked for a resource its sandbox does not permit, and Windows refused. The sandbox worked exactly as intended.
rules.why: This is the security boundary doing its job and reporting it. It is an audit record of a denial by design, not evidence of an attack or a broken app.
rules.action: Ignore.
falsepositives: Emitted constantly on any machine running Store or packaged apps.

rules.title: Windows could not verify one of the standard user folders
rules.plain: Windows checked one of the standard shell folders (Desktop, Documents and so on) and was refused access, usually with error 0x80070005 - access denied.
rules.why: Occasional denials during profile setup or folder redirection are normal. Persistent ones can mean the folder permissions are genuinely wrong, which breaks Save dialogs and folder redirection.
rules.action: Read the path named in the event. If it is a real user folder, compare its NTFS permissions and ownership against a working profile.
falsepositives: Common and harmless during first sign-in, profile creation and OneDrive folder moves.

rules.title: Windows could not create one of the standard user folders
rules.plain: Windows tried to create a standard shell folder and was denied, usually with 0x80070005 - access denied.
rules.why: Same family as the verification failure, but at creation time. Repeated failures for a folder a user needs surface as missing or unusable locations in Explorer.
rules.action: Read the path from the event and check whether it exists with sane permissions.
falsepositives: Routine for per-app folders under ProgramData that a non-admin process is not allowed to create.

rules.title: Leftover app files could not be deleted yet
rules.plain: After removing or updating a Store app, Windows could not delete some files because something still had them open. They are moved to a Deleted folder and cleaned up later.
rules.why: Deferred cleanup is the designed behaviour. The disk space is reclaimed on a later pass.
rules.action: Ignore.
falsepositives: Normal after any Store app update or removal.

rules.title: Telemetry upload could not reach Microsoft
rules.plain: The Windows telemetry client could not complete a connection during its last reporting period.
rules.why: Expected on machines that are offline, behind a proxy, on metered connections, or that have telemetry restricted by policy. It says nothing about the health of the machine itself.
rules.action: Ignore. If telemetry is deliberately blocked by policy or firewall, this is the expected result.
falsepositives: Guaranteed on any machine where telemetry endpoints are blocked by policy, firewall or hosts file.

rules.title: Settings sync component reported an error
rules.plain: The component that syncs Windows settings and Start menu layout between devices logged an internal error, commonly 0x80040154 - class not registered.
rules.why: CloudStore is noisy by nature and its failures are usually confined to settings roaming. It appears in bulk on machines not signed into a Microsoft account.
rules.action: Ignore unless Start menu layout or settings roaming is visibly broken.
falsepositives: Expected in volume on machines with no Microsoft account or with settings sync disabled.

rules.title: A WMI query failed
rules.plain: Something queried WMI and the query failed. The event names the client process, the namespace, the query and the result code.
rules.why: Individually these are usually a poorly written query or a class that does not exist on this edition of Windows. In volume from one process, that process is repeatedly asking for something it will never get.
rules.action: Group by ClientProcess in the event detail. A single process dominating the count is the thing to fix.
falsepositives: Monitoring agents and inventory tools generate these routinely by probing for optional classes.

rules.title: PowerShell script block logging is recording executed code
rules.plain: Script block logging is enabled, so Windows writes the text of every PowerShell script block that runs into the event log.
rules.why: This is a security auditing feature working as configured, not a fault. It matters for two reasons: it is a large share of log volume, and the recorded script text can contain secrets that were passed inline.
rules.action: Nothing to fix. Treat the recorded script text as sensitive. Note that running LogVerdict itself generates these entries.
falsepositives: Every PowerShell-based management tool, including LogVerdict, adds to this count.

rules.title: PowerShell 7 script block logging is recording executed code
rules.plain: The same script block logging as Windows PowerShell, emitted by PowerShell 7 into its own channel.
rules.why: Expected when script block logging is enabled by policy. The captured text can include base64-encoded commands, which look alarming but are how many legitimate tools pass scripts.
rules.action: Nothing to fix. An encoded command is not evidence of wrongdoing on its own; decode it if the origin is unclear.
falsepositives: Encoded commands are routine for scheduled tasks, installers and management tooling.

rules.title: A Remote Desktop session disconnected
rules.plain: The Remote Desktop client recorded a disconnection and its reason code.
rules.why: Normal at the end of every RDP session. Meaningful only if sessions are dropping unexpectedly mid-work.
rules.action: Ignore unless users report RDP sessions dropping. If they do, the error code distinguishes a network drop from a server-side disconnect.
falsepositives: Logged on every normal session close, including deliberate sign-out.

rules.title: A storage command failed
rules.plain: The storage diagnostic component recorded a failed SCSI request to a drive.
rules.why: Storage commands do fail benignly, particularly against removable media and virtual disks. A sustained rate against a fixed internal disk is a different matter and belongs with the other disk findings in this report.
rules.action: Correlate with any disk or Ntfs findings above. If those are present too, treat the drive as suspect and check its SMART data.

escalate.why: A sustained rate of failed storage commands points at failing media rather than incidental errors.

falsepositives: Removable drives, card readers and virtual disks produce these routinely.

rules.title: Microsoft Store internal timer bookkeeping
rules.plain: The Store app tried to cancel an internal timer that was no longer in its table.
rules.why: Purely internal housekeeping inside the Store app. It has no user-visible effect.
rules.action: Ignore.
falsepositives: Emitted in volume whenever the Store app is running.

rules.title: Windows could not decrypt some stored protected data
rules.plain: DPAPI - the service that protects saved passwords, certificates and app secrets - failed to unprotect a blob. "MAC check failed" means the data did not match the key used to decrypt it.
rules.why: Usually the data was encrypted under a different user profile, a since-changed password, or a profile restored from backup. Users experience it as saved credentials that silently stop working.
rules.action: If users report saved passwords or certificates disappearing, this is the mechanism. Re-saving the affected credentials is the practical fix; the old data is not recoverable.
falsepositives: Expected after a profile restore, a domain migration, or an administrative password reset.

rules.title: Windows blocked a program from loading unsigned or mismatched code
rules.plain: Code Integrity refused to let a process load a file because it did not meet the signing policy in force.
rules.why: This is a security control working. It matters because it also breaks legitimate software: the blocked component simply does not load, and the application may then fail in confusing ways.
rules.action: Read the blocked file path from the event. If it belongs to software you trust and that software is misbehaving, the vendor shipped an unsigned or incorrectly signed component.
falsepositives: Browsers and games with self-updating components trigger this routinely without any real problem.

rules.title: An exploit mitigation stopped a process doing something unsafe
rules.plain: A Windows exploit mitigation - such as arbitrary code guard or hardware-enforced shadow stacks - blocked an operation in a running process. The event names the process.
rules.why: Mitigations fire on legitimate software too, especially browsers, games and anything using just-in-time compilation. A block is not evidence of an attack, but a process blocked repeatedly may be crashing or degraded.
rules.action: Read the process name. If that application is unstable, its mitigation policy is a likely cause and can be tuned in Exploit Protection settings.
falsepositives: Browsers, Steam, Electron apps and JIT-based runtimes trigger these during entirely normal operation.

rules.title: Windows Hello for Business was not set up, by design
rules.plain: Windows checked whether it should start Windows Hello for Business provisioning, decided not to, and recorded why.
rules.why: This is a decision record, not a failure. On a machine that is not Entra joined or has no Hello policy, declining to provision is correct.
rules.action: Ignore unless Windows Hello for Business is supposed to be deployed here, in which case the event states which prerequisite was not met.
falsepositives: Expected on every machine that is not Entra joined or hybrid joined.

rules.title: Push notification service could not be reached
rules.plain: The Windows push notification client could not reach its service, commonly with 0x800704CF - the network location cannot be reached.
rules.why: Expected whenever the machine is offline, on a restricted network, or has notification endpoints blocked. It affects toast notifications only.
rules.action: Ignore unless Store app notifications are expected to work and do not.
falsepositives: Guaranteed on offline machines and networks that block Microsoft notification endpoints.

rules.title: A trace log filled up and started overwriting
rules.plain: A real-time event tracing session reached the maximum size of its backing file, so new events overwrite the oldest ones.
rules.why: This is a ring buffer behaving like a ring buffer. It matters only if you were relying on that specific trace for an investigation, because the oldest data is now gone.
rules.action: Ignore. If you need longer trace history for a specific investigation, increase that session buffer size before reproducing the problem.
falsepositives: Normal steady-state behaviour for long-running trace sessions such as the Defender API logger.

rules.title: A background download stopped before finishing
rules.plain: The Background Intelligent Transfer Service abandoned a transfer job. BITS is what Windows Update and many installers use to download in the background.
rules.why: Individually harmless, because BITS retries. Persistent failures for the same URL mean whatever depends on that download never completes, which is a common hidden cause of updates that never install.
rules.action: Read the URL from the event. If it is a Windows Update endpoint and update failures also appear in this report, they are the same problem.
falsepositives: Expected on metered, intermittent or captive-portal networks.

rules.title: An app deployment call arrived during shutdown
rules.plain: A component tried to start the app deployment service and got 0x8007045B, which means the system is shutting down.
rules.why: A race at shutdown between a component wanting to do app work and the system stopping services. It resolves itself on the next boot.
rules.action: Ignore.
falsepositives: Expected around shutdown and restart.

rules.title: App install agent could not read a settings cache
rules.plain: The install agent could not read a configuration value from its local cache of Microsoft-hosted settings, so it used the default.
rules.why: Falling back to a default is the designed behaviour. It has no effect on whether apps install.
rules.action: Ignore.
falsepositives: Common on machines with restricted network access to Microsoft settings endpoints.

rules.title: A storage reliability query was not supported
rules.plain: A storage management call failed, commonly a request for a drive reliability counter that the device does not implement.
rules.why: Many consumer NVMe and USB devices do not expose the reliability counters Windows asks for. The failure is the device declining to answer, not a fault.
rules.action: Ignore. To read drive health, use the vendor tool or SMART data directly.
falsepositives: Normal for USB enclosures, card readers and many consumer NVMe drives.

rules.title: Windows searched for a driver and did not find a better one
rules.plain: Device Setup Manager looked for a driver for a device and recorded the outcome of the search.
rules.why: Routine background driver maintenance. Only interesting when a device is genuinely non-functional, in which case it shows Windows has nothing better to offer.
rules.action: Ignore unless a device is not working, in which case the driver has to come from the vendor.
falsepositives: Emitted routinely during normal driver maintenance for working devices.

rules.title: An app package manifest uses an outdated schema
rules.plain: A Store app package declares a namespace or element that the current packaging schema no longer applies.
rules.why: A developer-facing compatibility notice about how the app was built. It does not stop the app working.
rules.action: Ignore. There is nothing an administrator can act on.
falsepositives: Normal for apps built against older Windows SDKs.

rules.title: WMI activity error
rules.plain: The WMI activity channel recorded a failure that does not match a more specific rule.
rules.why: WMI errors are dominated by tools probing for classes that do not exist on this machine. The client process named in the event detail is the useful part.
rules.action: Identify the client process from the event. If one process dominates the count, it is misconfigured or probing for something unavailable.
falsepositives: Inventory and monitoring agents generate these continuously while healthy.
